Subject: Private deployment connectivity options for Northgate

Hi Irene,

Thanks for taking this. We're evaluating Redwood Private for an on-prem inference cluster and need help choosing between VPC peering, PrivateLink (interface endpoints), or a persistent site-to-site VPN. Key constraints:
- Strong IP visibility requirements for auditing (source IP preservation)
- Regulated data residency and minimal egress exposure
- Predictable latency for inference (95th percentile < 30ms)
- Procurement needs clear ops runbook and SLAs to approve monthly billing

Can you provide a concise risk matrix and operational checklist that the Northgate network team can review? Also, any known vendor limits (PrivateLink concurrent connections, peering route table scale, NAT constraints) would be helpful.

Sam
Sam Walters
Head of Platform Engineering, Northgate Systems
procurement@northgate.com
From: Irene Choi <irene_choi@redwood.example>
To: Sam Walters <sam.walters@northgate.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.example>, Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.example>
Date: 2027-10-04T09:03:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Private deployment connectivity options for Northgate

Sam — thanks for the clear constraints. Attached is a short risk matrix and a network diagram (see attachments). High-level summary here:

- VPC peering
  - Pros: full L3 connectivity, straightforward for IP visibility and source-IP preservation (no NAT when configured). Low operational complexity once routes are in place.
  - Cons: Cross-account peering may require extended route table management across many prefixes; not suitable if you need private endpoints across multiple regions without VPC transitive routing. Peering doesn’t scale well as number of spoke VPCs grows.

- PrivateLink (interface endpoints)
  - Pros: Narrower surface area, strong security boundary (only specific services exposed). Good for least-privilege access and limits blast radius. Works well when you want to control egress paths and isolate RBAC.
  - Cons: Endpoint ENI count and per-AZ scaling constraints. Source-IP preservation is typically lost at the endpoint — you’ll see the ENI IPs unless you use additional proxying that preserves headers. Also, higher per-GB cost in some clouds.

- Site-to-site VPN
  - Pros: Familiar for on-premops teams, supports encrypted tunnels and BGP. Can preserve source IP depending on NAT configuration, but often requires NAT to avoid overlap. Good fallback for DR or transient connectivity.
  - Cons: Latency jitter and throughput limits on managed VPNs; not ideal for 95th percentile latency targets without direct interconnect. Ops overhead for BGP and failover testing.

Recommendation (short): Start with PrivateLink if your primary goal is a minimal attack surface and strict resource-level exposure. If you need guaranteed low-latency and full source-IP fidelity across many services, VPC peering (or a direct interconnect) is preferable. Keep a site-to-site VPN as a DR/fallback and for teams that require on-prem BGP integration.

Next steps:
1) I'll run a quick security/compliance checklist and mark operational steps for each option.
2) Ben — can you flag any kernel/driver/throughput caveats or ENI scaling numbers we should include?
3) Kimberly — can you draft procurement language for an SLA + fallback credits wording (DocuSign link to follow)?

Attachments: connectivity-risk-matrix.xlsx, network-diagram-v2.png

Thanks,
Irene Choi
Senior Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

On Mon, Oct 4, 2027 at 08:12 Sam Walters <sam.walters@northgate.com> wrote:
> Hi Irene,
> 
> Thanks for taking this. We're evaluating Redwood Private for an on-prem inference cluster...

Notes:
- PrivateLink performance: per-AZ endpoint ENIs + bandwidth limits. For high-volume inference we often hit per-ENI throughput ceilings unless we spread clients across multiple endpoints and AZs. That adds complexity for sticky sessions and KV cache locality.
- VPC peering: no NAT by default -> good for source IP preservation. But cross-account routing: careful with route table scale. Peering also doesn't provide the service-level abstraction that gives you fine-grained control over which subnets can reach the service.
- VPN: managed IPSec tunnels typically show higher jitter and can degrade 95p latency. For inference at scale we'd recommend Direct Connect / ExpressRoute when possible for latency and consistency.
- Observability: PrivateLink can complicate token-level attribution if the endpoint IPs are reused across customers. Make sure to add token-mapper headers or pass client identifiers at the application layer.

I'll add these to the risk matrix and a short ops checklist (tuning ENI counts, ALB placement, KV cache affinity strategies).

— Ben

Sam — quick answers and next steps inline:

1) Source IP preservation:
   - VPC peering: preserves source IP end-to-end (no NAT) when subnets and routing are configured accordingly.
   - PrivateLink: does not preserve client source IP by default; traffic terminates on endpoint ENIs. If you need source IP, we recommend either: (a) application-level client-id headers, or (b) place a proxy in your VPC that forwards original IPs via X-Forwarded-For and uses mutual TLS for auth.
   - S2S VPN: can preserve source IP depending on NAT configuration; overlapping address spaces often force NAT.

2) PrivateLink throughput: rough guidance for a 3-AZ AWS-style deployment:
   - Per-ENI baseline: expect ~0.5–1.5 Gbps practical throughput depending on instance type and cloud limits.
   - To support bursty inference at 95p latency <30ms you likely need multiple endpoints and AZ-level balancing. We'll include a sizing worksheet in the POC pack.

3) VPN failover runbook (abbreviated):
   - Step 1: Unhealthy detection: monitor latency/jitter thresholds > threshold for 3 consecutive probes (owned by Northgate NetOps).
   - Step 2: Initiate failover: switch BGP-preferred path to VPN tunnel A (Northgate) and notify Redwood on-call.
   - Step 3: Scale endpoints / enable extra ENIs if degraded (Redwood infra).
   - Step 4: Post-mortem: collect pcap, CloudWatch/Datadog traces, token-level attribution to confirm no token leakage during failover (joint responsibility).

I'll prepare the POC pack with: risk matrix, sizing worksheet, failover runbook, and a 2-week POC acceptance test. Ben and Jonas will add the observability hooks and ENI-scaling guidance. Kimberly will route the DocuSign when the POC SOW is ready.

Action owners:
- Redwood infra: Ben (ENI scaling + throughput), Jonas (observability hooks)
- Redwood sales/procurement: Kimberly (SLA + DocuSign)
- Northgate: Sam (NetOps contacts + test IP ranges)

Thanks — we'll send the POC pack by EOD tomorrow.
